subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Whereas the need for establishment of national highways is greater than in 1919;
And whereas in that year the Dominion government recognized its responsibility in this matter by a substantial grant, which grant is now exhausted,
Therefore be it resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should consider the advisability that a further federal grant be made to cover the next five years' development of highway construction.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, legislation was
passed in 1919 which provided for something similar to what this resolution asks for. Under that legislation provision was made for a grant of 880,000 a year to each of the provinces, and an additional amount based upon the population of each province, involving in its entirety the sum of 820,000,000. That scheme ran for a period of several years until all the money voted under that legislation had been used or was withdrawn by the government, At the present time the opinion is largely held in the Dominion of Canada that similar legislation should be introduced and additional financial aid provided for. A resolution similar to the one I now propose was passed by the United Farmers of Alberta, and I may say that I put this resolution on the order paper at their suggestion and request. Many other organizations have taken action along the same lines. Only a day or two ago such a resolution reached me from the Alberta Hotdlmen's Association. In addition I have received many private letters urging that parliament be asked to vote money for road construction. I might point out that when in 1919 parliament voted the original grant there was not the need for highways (hat there is to-day. At that time the automobile was not used to any great extent, and consequently there was not nearly the demand that we have to-day for expenditure on highway construction.
There is a certain body of opinion growing lip throughout the country that the federal government is more or less sidestepping its obligations in this regard. We have had experience of the federal government intiating such movements as this, but after contributing to the cost for a year or two they have stepped out and left the burden entirely on the provincial governments, which find themselves unable to carry the load. I am not making this criticism in a partisan spirit, foi I realize that members on both sides of the house are ready to support such legislation

National Highways-Mr. Kellner
as the resolution calls for; but I do think the federal government is very unfair when it starts the building of highways on a large scale and then, having led the people to believe that the grants will be continued from year to year, suddenly shifts the whole load on to the provinces. What makes it more difficult for the provinces to carry the burden is that with the steady flow of immigration into the west our provincial governments have to provide market roads, schools and other public works incidental to colonization.
There is no question but what the federal government is not using good business judgment in refusing to be a party to further expenditure on highways. For instance, national parks are being established in Alberta and the other western provinces, but no provision is made for access to them by tourists. Manifestly this is bad practice, and I am afraid that if we are to rely on the provincial governments providing the necessary roads it will be a long time before tourists and others will be able to reach these places of pleasure and beauty.
Then there is the further consideration of haulage costs. A thorough investigation in the United States has demonstrated that on a good substantial highway the cost to the farmer of hauling his grain to the railroad station is about one-third the cost of similar haulage over an ordinary dirt road. I believe this saving alone would justify the government in making a very substantial contribution towards the construction of good roads in western Canada.
To-night we have listened to a rather lengthy debate on the rights of the various provinces, and I think we must conclude that some consideration must be given to the taking of such steps as will tend to bind the provinces together into one national unit. Undoubtedly by providing main highways that will obviate the necessity of crossing over into the United States in making a trip from eastern to western Canada, we would be acting in the national interest. It is bad enough for a motorist not to be able to take a transcontinental trip across Canada; but even when he reaches the prairie provinces via the United States, if he is unfortunate enough to encounter wet weather, it is very doubtful if he will be able to make any satisfactory progress over our western roads. The expenditure of a reasonable amount of money would undoubtedly stimulate tourist traffic and be of substantial benefit to the local residents.
Let me point out that the federal government itself has a number of employees in
Allberta, Saskaohewan and Manitoba who use automobiles in the discharge of their official duties, and I doubt very much if it is not costing the federal treasury considerable extra expenditure on account of the time these men waste in getting out of mud holes. I recollect seeing an inspector for the Soldier Settlement Board spending days in travelling a few miles by reason of the bad condition of the roads. Therefore the federal government would benefit directly from having better roads in these provinces.
We admit that primarily the responsibility is on the provinces to build roads; but certainly it is not entirely there. These roads are more or less portions of a main highway across the country, and will benefit not only tourists but immigrants coming in from the United States and bound for the Peace River country. These roads also form part of the main highway which will enable Canadians to motor from east to west and from west to east without detouring through the United 'States. Now it would be unthinkable to have 'such main highways built in sections, a part by one province and another part by another province. I think you would have a very difficult time to get the various provinces to 'agree on just where and how such a road Should be constructed. Manifestly the federal 'government must undertake the construction to get the best results.
I want to go back to a remark I made in the first place about the large number of people in Canada who are in favour of an expenditure of this kind. I fancy that if a vote could be taken on this question alone a very large majority would be recorded in support of it. I think beyond a doubt that practically every section in Canada would support an expenditure such as this resolution suggests. And when we remember that in the last analysis it is the people of Canada who provide the money-the government is, of course, entrusted with the disposition of it-their opinion must surely influence the administration. Now, Mr. Speaker, the time for adjournment is getting near at hand and I will therefore conclude so as to give to some other hon. members who are in favour of the resolution an opportunity to express their views.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
I have very great pleasure in supporting the resolution moved by the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner). He has stated the case very fairly and mildly. I intend to take up but a very few minutes of the time of the house. It is time that Canada had a national high-

Nationat Highways-Mr. Coote
way. In the last few years we have claimed to be a nation and yet we have no highway; we have not even a road over which the people of eastern Canada can travel to the west or the people from the west visit the east. There is a large section of country in northern Ontario through which we have no highway at all.
I believe it is Henry Ford who has said that there is nothing in history which has contributed so much to the education of the people as the automobile. A good many people who never got away from home before are now using their cars, and I do not think there is anything that educates the people so much as getting away from their own locality and seeing some of the other sections of their own country. There are many people living in eastern Canada who perhaps will never visit the west until we provide a highway for them.
Let me suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that we have a very good reason for asking him to make further provision for federal aid to highways. The minister has for several years-in fact, ever since he became minister-maintained an excise tax on automobiles. The automobile to-day is a necessity, and I do not know of any other necessity in Canada which is singled out for an excise tax. For the fiscal years from 1919 to 1927 inclusive the federal government has collected through the excise tax on automobiles the sum of $34,722,000; and in that period it has given to the provinces, by way of federal aid to highways, the sum of $20,000,000. That leaves on hand in the treasury the sum of $14,722,000 as the balance realized from the excise tax on automobiles. Automobiles are no good to anyone unless there are roads over which to run them. The federal government has not contributed a dollar towards the construction of highways except through this federal aid to provincial highways, and I think that the federal government, since it has singled out the automobile for excise tax, should at least continue federal aid to highways until it has expended all the money which has been collected through thai tax. I do not think the government can find any good excuse for retaining this excise tax on automobiles unless it makes some such disposition of the money.
May I direct the attention of the minister to a comparison between the aid which this government has given to the provinces for highways and the aid given by the federal government in the United States for the same purpose. In this country we have contributed $20,000,000 as federal aid to highways; in the ]Mr. Coote.]
United States they have granted $650,000,000 in federal aid to highways. The comparison is very much in favour of the United States government, even when you take into
account their large population, the wealth of the -country and the revenues of that government.
Our government has assured us in the speech from the throne that the country is very prosperous, and I believe it could afford now to bring in another bill for the purpose suggested -in this resolution. That is the way it should be done; there should still be a bill providing for further aid to these highways. It might be wise in that bill to see that some provision is made for the construction of this all-Canadian highway, which we -might call Jubilee highway. It would be a splendid way of celebrating the jubilee of confederation.
The Minister of Finance is certainly very careful of the treasury; he is taking good care to see that it is not raided by the provinces in connection with highways. I heard someone suggest not long ago that he should be known as the Scotch Minister of Finance; he was getting to be about as careful as the Scotchman who refused to send his children to school because, as he said, they had to " ipay attention." I do hope that the Minister of Finance will open his heart a little and use some of this money he is collecting in these prosperous times to grant further aid to highways, especially -in view of the fact that he holds in the treasury possibly fifteen or sixteen million dollars which he has collected through the excise tax on automobiles.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
In twenty years' experience in this house I have observed that we generally start the session with resolutions advising the government to spend more money, and sometimes, even recently, we have closed the house with resolutions condemning the government for spending so much -money. We a-re starting this year true to form; I do not know how it will end. I do not know whether we shall have similar resolutions in the last days of the session, finding fault with expenditures, or whether the house will unanimously approve of the estimates that we have presented.
Now it is an easy matter, it is popular, in districts to suggest the spending of government money; every member of parliament knows that. Those of us who are in parliament, whether we sit to the right or to the left of the Speaker, when occasionally we have to face the electors are condemned by our opponents because we have been so long

National Highways-Mr. Robb
in the house and have never got anything for the county. The duty of the Minister of Finance is to see to it that there is a proper balance and that the country gets along without going into the money markets to borrow. When the highways bill was introduced in 1919, I believe, the then minister of railways, who brought in that measure, offered certain reasons why we should give aid to highways.
I recall that at that time two hon. members from western Canada challenged the constitutionality of voting money for highways. The matter never was pressed, 'but I remember that the issue was raised as to whether this federal parliament should vote money for that purpose, and it was pointed out that under the bili we were not only authorizing the expenditure of money 'by this parliament but were compelling the provinces to spend more money and consequently increase their rates of taxation. At that time the principal reason given for aid to highways was that it would provide a source of employment for returned soldiers, many of whom were out of work; it was argued by the then government that the expenditure of money in this way would aid employment throughout Canada. It was also pointed out that it would increase the tourist traffic, bringing more people to our country and increasing the expenditure of money here.
The conditions which prevailed in 1919 are quite different from those prevailing to-day, Mr. Speaker. In 1919 we had not quite realized the enormous debt of the country; we had not realized that every year the amount of money required for pensions would be increased; we had not realized that in 1928 we would have to write off some $16,000,000 which the returned soldiers claimed they had overpaid in the purchase of land and equipment for their farms. In 1919 the provinces did not have the revenues they now enjoy, and let me submit-not by way of reading a lesson but as a statement of fact-that we are elected to this house to look after federal finances and not to secure more money for the provinces to spend. Putting it before you in that way, as federal members elected by the people to look after federal finances, I submit that today the provinces are in a comparatively better position financially than the Dominion. The provinces have none of the expenses of the war to look after; the provincial bills for pensions to returned soldiers are not growing every year; the provinces do not have to pay interest on the enormous war debt of Canada, and because of the prosperity prevailing throughout Canada the provinces are now enjoying a much larger revenue than
they did in 1919. My hon. friend sitting beside me reminds me that the provinces have a further revenue from the liquor trade. I am not questioning that; it is perfectly legitimate business authorized by the people, and each province reports a profit from that trade.

When the Minister of Railways pointed out in 1919 that this work would give employment to returned soldiers and would result in an increased tourist trade he was probably quite correct, because the estimated statistics of the tourist traffic last year show that tourists coming into Canada spent in this country about $200,000,000, and

My hon. friend (Mr. Kellner) was elected as a federal member and he has voiced the opinion of his part of the country very frankly in saying that he is doing it at the request of an organization of hotel-keepers which met and passed a resolution that the government give assistance. Other organizations have met throughout the country and have urged that we give grants to education. We would like to give grants to education, but we come back to the real point:	The constitution determines what are properly federal obligations and what are properly provincial obligations. Until we have reduced the debt further and have been able to reduce the taxes upon the people, it seems to me that this matter might very well stand. For that reason I shall vote against the motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
I have 'listened to the hon.
Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) this evening and he certainly has not put forward any good reason why this grant should not be made. We are federal members dealing with interprovincial matters, and what is sought is aid to interprovincial highways. No one is seeking aid for local highways throughout the provinces; the words used by the hon. member (Mr. Kellner) in his resolution are "national highways". He is not seeking aid for little ten-mile highways running out of the villages; he is seeking recognition on the part of this parliament of the federal obligation with respect to highways.
The federal obligation with respect to highways is different to-day from what it was when the constitution was framed in 1867. Transportation is an entirely different thing from what it was then. In those days we had no motor cars, we had no bus lines, nor did we have any improved highways in the sense in which we use that term. If the minister will reflect a moment it will be abundantly clear to him that the bus lines of to-day take the place of the pioneer railways of yesterday. Bus lines are being operated from one part of this country to the other; they run not only within provinces but from one province to another. In the days gone by we aided the construction of railways through subsidies of $2,000 to $6,000 a mile in order that new territory might be opened up and transportation facilities provided for the pioneer. This new method of general transportation by motor vehicles, and the providing of facilities for tourists to travel in their own cars from one end of the country to the other, should be aided by a federal grant. In doing this no difficulty from a

National Highways-Mr. Bennett
constitutional standpoint is involved, because, as was stated by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) not long ago, it is a recognized constitutional axiom that this parliament may grant money for any purpose it desires. It has the right to collect taxes by any method, and it has the right to allocate those revenues to any particular purpose it may select. It may be a highway to-day, it may be education to-morrow; it may be the Boy Scouts, it may be the Girl Guides, or it may be some organization in Toronto which is looking after the health of the people. This parliament can in its wisdom and in the exercise of its discretion grant money for any purpose it pleases, whether it be in a province or a municipality or otherwise. Only last year the minister himself submitted to us an estimate by which a large sum of money was granted to erect some cribbing work to prevent the water wearing down the banks of a river. It was said by some that this was purely a provincial or municipal matter, but parliament has the right to do as it pleases with the money collected from the taxpayers, and the grant was made.
The minister has very properly said that the government will be held liable for the soundness of the discretion exercised and the wisdom displayed in the expenditure of the public money. There is no doubt about that. The Minister of Finance is the custodian of the public money; he is the keeper of the purse-strings of this country, and the government, with his guidance, must exercise its judgment and its discretion on the soundest possible line for the benefit of Canada as a whole. The minister invited us, as federal members, to consider our responsibility in the matter. I desire to remind him that our responsibility is not provincial, it is for Canada as a whole. In what better way could we help Canada than to make a substantia! grant in aid of national highways?
I put the following argument to the minister, and it seems to me that he should appreciate it more than any other member in this house:	It has been stated that over $200,-
000,000 was brought into this country by tourists during the last year.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: That is a very low estimate.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
I believe it has been put as high as $225,000,000.
M. RYCKMAN: Two hundred and sixty million.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
I will put it at $200,000,000 for the sake of argument. Does the Minister of Finance realize that that $200,000,000 redressed an adverse trade balance with the United States of America to the extent of practically that amount? Does he realize that that $200,000,000 brought in here from the United States made possible the maintenance of the Canadian dollar at par? Does he realize that every time an American tourist wrote out a cheque on an American trust or express company he was providing a sum which went to cancel an adverse balance against this country in the clearing houses of New York? That $200,000,000 is available in New York for the purpose of extinguishing our obligations for the payment of interest on municipal and provincial debentures. That is an important matter, and I suggest to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that if he will consult with the financial men of this country he will ascertain that the expenditure of that sum of money in Canada by these tourists had a very marked effect upon our exchange. If the Canadian dollar is maintained at par through this means, is it not important that this money should be expended? If that be so-and I think the minister will find it is true if he will consult the officers of his own department or the bankers of this country then the providing of efficient means of transportation will return very subtantial results through the increased tourist trade. I have no diffidence in saying that if support is thus given to a national highway system not provincial highways but highways between provinces, national in their character, if the Minister of Finance wifi appropriate a number of millions of dollars, probably in the supplementary estimates of this year, I am satisfied that the benefit to Canada will more than offset the expenditure made.
I confess that I have given more than a little attention to analyzing the figures with respect to the matter. It is not easy to put your finger on a given item of taxation and say: that has resulted from a certain expenditure made by the federal or the provincial treasury. It is not right to say that the gasoline tax, for instance, is able to take care of interprovincial obligations. The provinces have increased burdens imposed upon them by reason of the changed conditions under which they have to function and carry on government.
When the present Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) first undertook obligations in Saskatchewan, conditions had made much advance over what they were in 1905, but the advance in 1929 over conditions that existed when he took hold is as great as the
234	COMMONS
National Highways-Miss Macphail
preceding advance. We are steadily increasing the obligations of the provinces, the municipalities, and the only way in which one can hope to enable them to be in a position to provide great interprovincial systems of highways or roads that may be available for international traffic, for transportation for tourists, and thereby increase, as I have said, not only the ability of the people to pay, but the ability of the tourists to make their contribution to the adjustment of the adverse balances in connection with exchange, is by the Dominion itself making substantial contributions for the construction of those systems of national highways.
I would urge the minister to reconsider his attitude before he lightly asks parliament to vote down the resolution. It occurs to me that on mature consideration he will realize that this is not simply a grant given to a province, not a mere contribution, but an investment made by the Dominion of Canada that will pay large dividends and in a very short time, because of the increased sums that will be expended in this country and the greater purchasing power that will be made available for our citizens, repay the whole expenditure that may be made. The question of the amount received from excise taxes, sales taxes and matters of that kind I leave from my argument as being entirely beside the question. I put it on the broad, national ground of benefit to the country as a whole, the increased ability of the people to pay, and adjustments, by reason of increased tourist traffic, of adverse exchange balances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
My hon. friend admits now
that the people are better able to pay.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Did I not the other
afternoon say that the people were better able to pay? Did I not say that by reason of the vast crops of the country the people were better able to pay because of the larger purchasing power they have? Does the hon. gentleman for a single moment think any hon. member, because he happens to sit to the left of the Speaker, is not conscious of the fact that the vast crops have increased the ability of the people to pay? I am not the kind of gentleman he would make of himself if he sat to the left of the Speaker, because certainly he thinks it the duty of us to deny what every man who has eyes to see and ears to hear can observe. I am not one of those of whom it is said:	"Eyes have they, but
they see not: they have ears, but they hear not," lest seeing they might believe, and hearing they might understand. The very fact that the people have had that increase in prosperity and purchasing power on account of fMr. Bennett.]
the increase in agricultural wealth in Canada is an additional reason why more highways should be established to facilitate transportation, facilities that twenty-five or thirty years ago were railway facilities, that to-day are motor car facilities and that can be provided at this time only by aid from the federal exchequer.
Miss AGNES MACPHAIL (Southeast
Grey): I can say what I want to say on this subject before eleven o'clock. I think we all admit that one of the difficulties in Canada is that it is divided into two sections, one of which is cut off from the otheT, and surely the building of a highway would do something at least to hold Canada together as a unit. That spirit should find some expression, and I cannot think of a better way to do it than to build this highway. Those westerners who once lived in eastern Canada always used to come back in the winter time; but now since the automobile is so widely used they like to return in the summer, and this summer I heard at least a score of Canadians living both in the east and in the west say this very thing, namely, that they disliked having to go out of their own country in order to cross their own country. This is a condition which should be remedied.
While I am often convinced by the very sane arguments of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Roibb), I could not say that his speech to-night was very convincing. There were some expenditures of the last few years that he very carefully left untouched. If the Minister of Finance wanted to save money he could have done so last year in regard to the Quebec harbour vote. Everybody in Canada admits that a great deal of money was spent that need not have been spent. Parliament tried to stop it but the government would not have it stopped. The Holt-Gundy interests asked for a sum greater than $200,000 to dredge a channel from their harbour out to the main stream of the St. Lawrence, but they got that amount. Those are just two items that occur to me where money could have been saved. I am also reminded of the Ottawa Improvement Commission grants which amounted to quite a lot.
If we want more money, let us put the income tax back where it was two years ago. There is no reason why people with an income should not pay a tax on it. The bigger the income, the less they want to pay the tax, but the more we should see that they do pay it. If they pay the tax and if we save money on expenditures that are not necessary,

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
we certainly could build a highway across Canada. It would be a very good thing if Canadians knew more about their own country. I have often thought if hon. members who live in the east knew more about the west, and the other way around-particularly that way-it would be a splendid thing. If we had a highway, as almost everyone has a car, it would do very much to bring about a better feeling throughout Canada by making it possible for Canadians to know their own country. "See Canada first'1 might well become our slogan.

speechtext:
In the year 1919 a resolution was passed in the
house covering a grant of $20,000,000 for highways to be expended over a term of five years. This was the first movement in favour of good roads in the Dominon of Canada and it has had a Dominion-wide effect. The result is that the good roads movement was started and the provinces have spent or are spending forty or fifty times the amount of the original grant.
